JOINDER OF A THIRD PARTY (CLAIMANT) IN A CALIFORNIA FAMILY LAW CASE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Rosalind Amaya Okonkwo · Teodoro Okonkwo

PARTIES, SCOPE, AND PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This Third-Party Joinder Information Sheet concerns Rosalind Amaya Okonkwo and Teodoro Okonkwo in connection with the pending dissolution proceeding and the division of the community estate, a matter pending or to be filed in the California superior court for Sacramento County, and the position of Okonkwo Family Revocable Trust, a person or entity who is not one of the two parties to that case. California family law is organized almost entirely around a two-party case, and most published guidance addresses what the two parties may claim from each other. This sheet takes up a different question: who else may be made a party. It surveys Family Code section 2021, which authorizes joinder of a person who claims an interest in the proceeding; rule 5.24 of the California Rules of Court, which supplies the definitions, the categories of person who may seek joinder, the mandatory and permissive standards, the forms and the summons; the California Supreme Court's decision in Bianka M. v. Superior Court (2018) 5 Cal.5th 1004, which places rule 5.24 inside the general compulsory joinder statute, Code of Civil Procedure section 389; two published Court of Appeal decisions applying joinder to people who hold or claim community property, Glade v. Glade (1995) 38 Cal.App.4th 1441 and Babcock v. Superior Court (1994) 29 Cal.App.4th 721; and the separate statutory track that governs employee benefit plans, Family Code sections 2060 through 2074 and rule 5.29. It states what those authorities say and hold. It does not determine whether anyone may or should be joined in this case, does not recommend that joinder be sought or opposed, does not predict how a court would rule, and is not a substitute for advice from a lawyer licensed in California.

THE STATUTE: FAMILY CODE SECTION 2021 AND THE TWO TRACKS IT CREATES
Family Code section 2021 sits in the chapter of procedural provisions that applies to nullity, dissolution and legal separation proceedings. It has two subdivisions and creates two tracks. Subdivision (a) states that, subject to subdivision (b), the court may order that a person who claims an interest in the proceeding be joined as a party, in accordance with rules adopted by the Judicial Council under Family Code section 211. The statute itself therefore supplies no standard, no procedure and no form; it delegates all of that to the Rules of Court, which is why the operative law of third-party joinder in a family law case is found in rule 5.24 rather than in the Family Code. Subdivision (b) carves out one class of prospective party entirely: an employee benefit plan may be joined only in accordance with Chapter 6 of the same part, beginning at section 2060. The section's present wording dates from Statutes 1996, chapter 1061, section 3, effective January 1, 1997.

RULE 5.24: WHAT THE RULE COVERS, WHOSE LAW APPLIES, AND WHAT A "CLAIMANT" IS
Rule 5.24 of the California Rules of Court opens with a limiting sentence: a person who claims or controls an interest in any matter subject to disposition in the proceeding may be joined as a party to the family law case only as provided in that chapter. Subdivision (a)(1) then imports the general law: all provisions of law relating to joinder of parties in civil actions generally apply to joinder of a person as a party to a family law case, except as otherwise provided in the chapter. Subdivision (a)(2) goes further and detaches the joined portion of the case from family law procedure altogether: the law applicable to civil actions generally governs all pleadings, motions and other matters pertaining to that portion of the proceeding as to which a claimant has been joined, in the same manner as if a separate action not subject to the family rules had been filed, except as otherwise provided in the chapter or by the court in which the proceeding is pending. Subdivision (b) defines the term the rule uses throughout: a claimant is an individual or an entity joined, or sought or seeking to be joined, as a party to the family law proceeding. The definition is symmetrical — it covers a person someone else is trying to bring in and a person trying to come in.

WHO MAY ASK FOR JOINDER: THE PARTIES, AND TWO CLASSES OF PERSON WHO MAY JOIN THEMSELVES
Rule 5.24(c) names three groups. Under (c)(1), the petitioner or the respondent may apply for an order joining a person who has or claims custody or physical control of any of the minor children subject to the action, or visitation rights with respect to those children, or who has in his or her possession or control or claims to own any property subject to the jurisdiction of the court in the proceeding. The property branch of that sentence is the one that reaches a business, a trustee, a relative, a cohabitant or any other stranger to the marriage who is holding or claiming something the court will have to characterize. Under (c)(2), a person who has or claims custody or physical control of a minor child of the action, or visitation rights, may apply to join himself or herself — the rule allows self-joinder for the custody group without any application by a party. Under (c)(3), a person served with an order temporarily restraining the use of property that is in his or her possession or control or that he or she claims to own, or affecting custody or visitation, may likewise apply to join himself or herself. Subdivision (c)(3) is the rule's answer to a nonparty who is bound by a restraining order but has no standing in the case.

THE APPLICATION: FORM FL-371, THE ACCOMPANYING PLEADING, AND A DEFECT IN THE PUBLISHED RULE
Rule 5.24(d)(1) prescribes the vehicle. Every application for joinder other than one for an employee pension benefit plan must be made by serving and filing the Notice of Motion and Declaration for Joinder, Judicial Council form FL-371; the hearing date must be less than 30 days from the date the notice is filed; the completed form must state with particularity the claimant's interest in the proceeding and the relief the applicant seeks; and the form must be accompanied by an appropriate pleading setting forth the claim as if it were asserted in a separate action or proceeding. That last requirement is the practical counterpart of subdivision (a)(2): the claim against the claimant is pleaded in civil form. Rule 5.24(d)(2) requires that a blank copy of the Responsive Declaration to Motion for Joinder and Consent Order for Joinder, form FL-373, be served with the notice of motion and the accompanying pleading.

MANDATORY JOINDER: THE ONE CATEGORY THE COURT MUST BRING IN
Rule 5.24(e)(1) is headed "Mandatory joinder" and describes a duty, not a discretion. Under (e)(1)(A), the court must order that a person be joined as a party if the court discovers that the person has physical custody of, or claims custody or visitation rights with respect to, any minor child of the marriage or domestic partnership, or any minor child of the relationship. The trigger is the court's discovery of the fact or the claim, not a request by a party. Under (e)(1)(B), before ordering the joinder of a grandparent of a minor child under Family Code section 3104, the court must first take the actions described in section 3104(a). Nothing in subdivision (e)(1) speaks to property: the only category the rule makes mandatory is the custody and visitation category.

PERMISSIVE JOINDER: INDISPENSABLE TO THE ISSUE, OR NECESSARY TO ENFORCEMENT, PLUS FOUR FACTORS
Rule 5.24(e)(2), headed "Permissive joinder," states a two-part test. The court may order that a person be joined if it finds, first, that it would be appropriate to determine the particular issue in the proceeding, and second, that the person to be joined is either indispensable for the court to make an order about that issue or is necessary to the enforcement of any judgment rendered on that issue. The rule then tells the court how to decide the first part. In deciding whether it is appropriate to determine the particular issue in the proceeding, the court must consider the effect on the proceeding, including whether resolving the issue will unduly delay disposition; whether other parties would need to be joined to make an effective judgment between the parties; whether resolving the issue will confuse other issues in the proceeding; and whether joinder of a party to determine the particular issue will complicate, delay or otherwise interfere with the effective disposition of the proceeding. Every one of the four listed considerations is about the burden joinder places on the existing case rather than about the strength of the claimant's claim.

WHAT HAPPENS AFTER THE COURT ORDERS JOINDER: SUMMONS FL-375 AND THIRTY DAYS TO RESPOND
Rule 5.24(e)(3) sets out what follows an order of joinder. If the court orders that a person be joined as a party under the rule, the court must direct that a summons be issued on the Summons (Joinder), form FL-375, and that the claimant be served with a copy of the Notice of Motion and Declaration for Joinder (form FL-371), the pleading attached to it, the order of joinder, and the summons. The claimant then has 30 days after service to file an appropriate response. Joinder is therefore not complete when the order is signed: a summons issues and is served, the way it would be in a separate civil action, which is the procedural expression of the principle stated in subdivision (a)(2) that civil rules govern the joined portion of the case.

BIANKA M. V. SUPERIOR COURT (2018): RULE 5.24 OPERATES INSIDE CODE OF CIVIL PROCEDURE SECTION 389
In Bianka M. v. Superior Court the California Supreme Court reviewed an order requiring a child who had filed a parentage action to join her nonresident father as a party before the court would rule on her requests. The Court framed the joinder question in general civil terms. It stated that in civil litigation generally the question whether a person must be joined as a party to a suit is governed by the compulsory joinder statute, Code of Civil Procedure section 389; that if such a person, sometimes called a necessary party, cannot be joined, subdivision (b) requires the court to consider whether in equity and good conscience the suit can proceed without the absent party; and that to guide implementation of these general joinder principles in the family law context the Judicial Council has promulgated rule 5.24. The Court then read the mandatory provision as a legislative identification of necessary parties: in a family law action, rule 5.24(e) identifies one category of persons who by definition are materially interested in the action and are therefore necessary parties — those who have physical custody of the child or make a claim to custody or visitation after being served with notice of the pending action. On the permissive provision, the Court said that all of rule 5.24(e)(2) appears to presuppose that joinder is in fact feasible, and that the rule does not expressly address what should happen when joinder is infeasible because, for example, the person to be joined is beyond the court's jurisdiction. The Court's disposition on this point was that, provided the absent parent has received adequate notice, the action may proceed even if the parent is beyond the personal jurisdiction of the court and cannot be joined as a party.

GLADE V. GLADE (1995): A STRANGER WHO CLAIMS COMMUNITY PROPERTY MAY BE JOINED, AND DUE PROCESS IS NOTICE AND A HEARING
Glade v. Glade arose when a family trust holding a note and deed of trust on the spouses' residence brought a foreclosure action while the dissolution was pending. The family law court joined the husband's parents and the trust and stayed the foreclosure; a different department of the same superior court granted the trust summary judgment. The Court of Appeal held the stay valid and the summary judgment beyond the second department's jurisdiction. Along the way the opinion sets out the joinder principle. It states that in Elms v. The Glade court adds that both the Family Code and the California Rules of Court grant the family law court broad powers to determine and characterize community property and join third parties with an interest in such property, and describes the baseline it is departing from by noting that the spouses are normally the only parties to a marital dissolution action. THE SEPARATE TRACK: JOINING AN EMPLOYEE BENEFIT PLAN UNDER FAMILY CODE SECTIONS 2060 THROUGH 2065
Family Code section 2021(b) sends employee benefit plans to their own chapter, and that chapter works differently from rule 5.24 in almost every respect. Under section 2060(a), joinder is ministerial rather than judicial: upon written application by a party, the clerk shall enter an order joining as a party any employee benefit plan in which either party claims an interest that is or may be subject to disposition by the court. Section 2063 gives the plan 30 days to file and serve a notice of appearance and makes a responsive pleading optional: the plan may but need not file one, and if it does not, all statements of fact and requests for relief in any pleading served on it are deemed controverted by the notice of appearance. Section 2064 exempts the plan from any filing fee for the notice of appearance or any later paper. Section 2065 supplies a default remedy if the plan is served and files nothing. WHAT A JOINED PLAN MAY DO, AND THE AUTOMATIC STAY ON ORDERS MADE WITHOUT IT
Family Code sections 2070 through 2074 govern the proceeding after a plan has been joined. Section 2072 sets the plan's posture: the plan is not required to, but may, appear at any hearing in the proceeding, and for purposes of the Code of Civil Procedure the plan is considered a party appearing at the trial with respect to any hearing at which the interest of the parties in the plan is an issue before the court. A plan may therefore sit out the case without forfeiting the procedural standing of an appearing party. Section 2073 protects it further. Provisions of an order entered by stipulation of the parties, or entered at or as a result of a hearing the plan did not attend, that affect the plan or affect any interest either spouse may have or claim under the plan, are stayed until 30 days after the order has been served on the plan. The plan may waive the period, may extend it to 60 days by filing and serving a request within the 30 days, and may file a motion within the period to set aside or modify the provisions affecting it, in which case those provisions remain stayed until the motion is resolved. Section 2074 allows any party to present further evidence at the hearing on such a motion on the rights of the parties under the plan or the extent of their community or quasi-community interest, unless the parties have agreed in writing otherwise. A reported illustration of a plan appearing in a dissolution is In re Marriage of Cooper (2008) 160 Cal.App.4th 574, where the opinion records that pursuant to Family Code section 2060 the California Public Employees' Retirement System was joined as a party to the proceedings in the trial court and was later granted permission to file an amicus curiae brief on appeal.

Family Code section 2021 sits in the chapter of procedural provisions that applies to nullity, dissolution and legal separation proceedings. It has two subdivisions and creates two tracks. Subdivision (a) states that, subject to subdivision (b), the court may order that a person who claims an interest in the proceeding be joined as a party, in accordance with rules adopted by the Judicial Council under Family Code section 211. The statute itself therefore supplies no standard, no procedure and no form; it delegates all of that to the Rules of Court, which is why the operative law of third-party joinder in a family law case is found in rule 5.24 rather than in the Family Code. Subdivision (b) carves out one class of prospective party entirely: an employee benefit plan may be joined only in accordance with Chapter 6 of the same part, beginning at section 2060. The section's present wording dates from Statutes 1996, chapter 1061, section 3, effective January 1, 1997.

Subdivision (a)(1) then imports the general law: all provisions of law relating to joinder of parties in civil actions generally apply to joinder of a person as a party to a family law case, except as otherwise provided in the chapter. Subdivision (b) defines the term the rule uses throughout: a claimant is an individual or an entity joined, or sought or seeking to be joined, as a party to the family law proceeding. The definition is symmetrical — it covers a person someone else is trying to bring in and a person trying to come in.

expectedJSON.body: Rule 5.24(e)(2), headed "Permissive joinder," states a two-part test. The court may order that a person be joined if it finds, first, that it would be appropriate to determine the particular issue in the proceeding, and second, that the person to be joined is either indispensable for the court to make an order about that issue or is necessary to the enforcement of any judgment rendered on that issue. The rule then tells the court how to decide the first part. In deciding whether it is appropriate to determine the particular issue in the proceeding, the court must consider the effect on the proceeding, including whether resolving the issue will unduly delay disposition; whether other parties would need to be joined to make an effective judgment between the parties; whether resolving the issue will confuse other issues in the proceeding; and whether joinder of a party to determine the particular issue will complicate, delay or otherwise interfere with the effective disposition of the proceeding. Every one of the four listed considerations is about the burden joinder places on the existing case rather than about the strength of the claimant's claim.

expectedJSON.body: In Bianka M. v. Superior Court the California Supreme Court reviewed an order requiring a child who had filed a parentage action to join her nonresident father as a party before the court would rule on her requests. The Court framed the joinder question in general civil terms. It stated that in civil litigation generally the question whether a person must be joined as a party to a suit is governed by the compulsory joinder statute, Code of Civil Procedure section 389; that if such a person, sometimes called a necessary party, cannot be joined, subdivision (b) requires the court to consider whether in equity and good conscience the suit can proceed without the absent party; and that to guide implementation of these general joinder principles in the family law context the Judicial Council has promulgated rule 5.24. The Court then read the mandatory provision as a legislative identification of necessary parties: in a family law action, rule 5.24(e) identifies one category of persons who by definition are materially interested in the action and are therefore necessary parties — those who have physical custody of the child or make a claim to custody or visitation after being served with notice of the pending action. On the permissive provision, the Court said that all of rule 5.24(e)(2) appears to presuppose that joinder is in fact feasible, and that the rule does not expressly address what should happen when joinder is infeasible because, for example, the person to be joined is beyond the court's jurisdiction. The Court's disposition on this point was that, provided the absent parent has received adequate notice, the action may proceed even if the parent is beyond the personal jurisdiction of the court and cannot be joined as a party.

expectedJSON.body: Glade v. Glade arose when a family trust holding a note and deed of trust on the spouses' residence brought a foreclosure action while the dissolution was pending. The family law court joined the husband's parents and the trust and stayed the foreclosure; a different department of the same superior court granted the trust summary judgment. The Court of Appeal held the stay valid and the summary judgment beyond the second department's jurisdiction. Along the way the opinion sets out the joinder principle. It states that in Elms v. Elms (1935) 4 Cal.2d 681 the Supreme Court confirmed that either spouse in a marital dissolution action may join third parties claiming an interest in alleged community property, and reproduces the Elms policy reasoning, including the observation that the court can scarcely make a fair distribution or allotment of parcels of community property without determining what property is community. The Glade court adds that both the Family Code and the California Rules of Court grant the family law court broad powers to determine and characterize community property and join third parties with an interest in such property, and describes the baseline it is departing from by noting that the spouses are normally the only parties to a marital dissolution action. On what the joined stranger is owed, Glade quotes In re Marriage of Davis (1977) 68 Cal.App.3d 294 for the proposition that the only limitation on the family court's jurisdiction over property held by a third party was the safeguarding of that person's right to due process of law, and that when she was given notice and a right to be heard, her due process rights were satisfied. The opinion's conclusion on the point is that once the marital dissolution action was underway, the family law court acquired jurisdiction over alleged community property in the hands of third parties and could properly order their joinder and the sale of that property.

expectedJSON.body: Babcock v. Superior Court is a writ proceeding brought by a woman living with one spouse while that spouse's dissolution was pending. The other spouse suspected that community funds had paid for the cohabitant's house and car, served subpoenas on banks and a dealership, and moved both to compel production and to join the cohabitant in the dissolution proceeding on the ground that community funds had been wrongfully diverted to her. The cohabitant sought a writ, arguing among other things that her joinder was improper. On that point the Court of Appeal was brief and categorical: joinder is proper where a spouse alleges that the other spouse has illegally made a gift of community funds, and the court denied the petition on the joinder issue, citing Family Code sections 1100, subdivision (b), and 2021 together with the then-current rule of court. The remainder of the opinion concerns the nonparty's privacy interest in her financial records and holds that the trial court abused its discretion by failing to conduct an in camera review and to issue a protective order; that is, the same opinion that allows the stranger to be made a party also limits what may be taken from her once she is one.

expectedJSON.body: Family Code section 2021(b) sends employee benefit plans to their own chapter, and that chapter works differently from rule 5.24 in almost every respect. Under section 2060(a), joinder is ministerial rather than judicial: upon written application by a party, the clerk shall enter an order joining as a party any employee benefit plan in which either party claims an interest that is or may be subject to disposition by the court. There is no motion, no hearing, no indispensability finding and no discretion. Section 2060(b) states the reason the step matters: an order or judgment in the proceeding is not enforceable against an employee benefit plan unless the plan has been joined as a party. Section 2061 requires the party requesting joinder, upon entry of the order, to file an appropriate pleading setting forth that party's claim against the plan and the nature of the relief sought. Section 2062 requires service on the plan of the pleading on joinder, the request and order of joinder, the summons (joinder) and a blank notice of appearance, and adds an information-forcing duty running between the spouses: to facilitate identification and service, the employee spouse must furnish to the nonemployee spouse within 30 days after written request, as to each employee benefit plan covering the employee, the name of the plan and the name, title, address and telephone number of the plan's trustee, administrator or agent for service of process. Section 2063 gives the plan 30 days to file and serve a notice of appearance and makes a responsive pleading optional: the plan may but need not file one, and if it does not, all statements of fact and requests for relief in any pleading served on it are deemed controverted by the notice of appearance. Section 2064 exempts the plan from any filing fee for the notice of appearance or any later paper. Section 2065 supplies a default remedy if the plan is served and files nothing. Rule 5.29 of the California Rules of Court fixes the forms for this track: the request for joinder and order on form FL-372 with the pleading on joinder on form FL-370, the summons on form FL-375, and the plan's notice of appearance and responsive pleading under section 2063(b) on form FL-374.

expectedJSON.body: Family Code sections 2070 through 2074 govern the proceeding after a plan has been joined. Section 2072 sets the plan's posture: the plan is not required to, but may, appear at any hearing in the proceeding, and for purposes of the Code of Civil Procedure the plan is considered a party appearing at the trial with respect to any hearing at which the interest of the parties in the plan is an issue before the court. A plan may therefore sit out the case without forfeiting the procedural standing of an appearing party. Section 2073 protects it further. Provisions of an order entered by stipulation of the parties, or entered at or as a result of a hearing the plan did not attend, that affect the plan or affect any interest either spouse may have or claim under the plan, are stayed until 30 days after the order has been served on the plan. The plan may waive the period, may extend it to 60 days by filing and serving a request within the 30 days, and may file a motion within the period to set aside or modify the provisions affecting it, in which case those provisions remain stayed until the motion is resolved. Section 2074 allows any party to present further evidence at the hearing on such a motion on the rights of the parties under the plan or the extent of their community or quasi-community interest, unless the parties have agreed in writing otherwise. A reported illustration of a plan appearing in a dissolution is In re Marriage of Cooper (2008) 160 Cal.App.4th 574, where the opinion records that pursuant to Family Code section 2060 the California Public Employees' Retirement System was joined as a party to the proceedings in the trial court and was later granted permission to file an amicus curiae brief on appeal.

expectedJSON.body: Several limits on the authorities collected here are worth stating plainly. First, the case law predates the current rule. Rule 5.24 was adopted effective January 1, 2013 and amended effective January 1, 2017, while Glade v. Glade (1995) and Babcock v. Superior Court (1994) construe the predecessor rules, principally former rule 1250 and, in Glade, former rules 1211(a), 1213, 1225 and 1254(a). Those opinions are quoted in this sheet for their reasoning about the family court's authority over strangers to the marriage, not for the rule text they recite. Second, the statutory hook is thin. Family Code section 2021 delegates rather than regulates, and the only judicial treatment of it located in this research is the single-sentence citation in Babcock; a full-text search for the phrase "Family Code section 2021" in the CourtListener opinion corpus returned no results. Third, the most recent controlling decision expressly reserved the central question. Bianka M. v. Superior Court assumed without deciding that the absent parent was a necessary party as to one requested finding, and rested instead on the infeasibility of joining him, so the Supreme Court has not said what makes a claimant indispensable under rule 5.24(e)(2). Fourth, the rule contains an unremedied textual defect in subdivision (d)(1) that both official publications carry. Fifth, none of the fetched authorities addresses the consequence of failing to join a person in the mandatory custody category, whether a court may order joinder on its own motion where nobody has applied, or what default consequence follows a joined claimant's failure to respond within the 30 days rule 5.24(e)(3) allows.
